provisioning:Mercado Municipal de Faro.name: Mercado Municipal de Faro
provisioning:Mercado Municipal de Faro.teaser: Faro's everyday market for the galley run: the day's fish, fruit, bread, and a bifana at the counter
provisioning:Mercado Municipal de Faro.story: Treat it as the practical run, not the show. Do the fish counters first, while the morning's catch is still on the ice, and buy for tonight only. Then fill the bags with fruit, vegetables and bread for the boat. Shopping done, stand at Snack Bar da Xica inside the hall for a bifana and a small beer. For a bigger fish choice, or Saturday stalls, go to Olhão.
provisioning:Mercado Municipal de Faro.why: Shop the fish before ten, then eat your bifana at the counter.
facts: The day's fish, fruit and vegetables, bread; a bifana at Snack Bar da Xica
Monday to Saturday mornings; go early (seen May 2026)
By the kilo and the season (seen May 2026)

provisioning:Mercado de Olhão.name: Mercado de Olhão
provisioning:Mercado de Olhão.teaser: Fish in the east hall, fruit in the west, and on Saturdays the growers set up outside before nine
provisioning:Mercado de Olhão.story: Come with a cool box and an open list. The east hall is the fish: sardines off the boats, octopus, Pacific oysters, amêijoa-boa clams from the lagoon. The west hall has the fruit and vegetables. On Saturday the region's growers also set up outside the halls, and that is the morning to come, before nine. Pick up a bag of Ria Formosa flor de sal on the way out.
provisioning:Mercado de Olhão.why: Saturday before nine, with ice in the cool box: buy the clams, then the vegetables outside.
facts: Sardines, octopus, Pacific oysters, amêijoa-boa clams; Ria Formosa salt and flor de sal; produce from the Saturday growers outside
Monday to Saturday, 07:00-13:00; Saturday before 09:00 is the morning (seen May 2026)
Sardines about EUR 4 a kilo (seen May 2026); otherwise by the catch

provisioning:Flor de sal de Tavira.name: Flor de sal de Tavira
provisioning:Flor de sal de Tavira.teaser: The thin top crust of the Tavira salt pans, raked off by hand in summer and sold with a DOP seal
provisioning:Flor de sal de Tavira.story: Flor de sal is the fragile skin of crystals that forms on the brine of the Ria Formosa salt pans on hot, still, dry days. Salt workers lift it off by hand between June and September with the borboleta, a butterfly-shaped wooden tool, then leave it to dry in the sun. Nothing is washed, refined or added, and the flakes crumble between the fingers. The salt of Tavira has a long paper trail: the old guide dates the Crown's claim on its salinas to Afonso III in 1266. Scatter it at the end, on grilled fish or a sliced tomato, never into the cooking water.
provisioning:Flor de sal de Tavira.why: A light, unbreakable present to carry home: check for the words Flor de Sal de Tavira and the DOP mark.
facts: The salt pans of the Ria Formosa around Tavira; bags at the Mercado de Olhão salt stalls

provisioning:Krater.name: Krater
provisioning:Krater.teaser: A small Portuguese wine shop on the Baixa's pedestrian Rua Conselheiro Bívar, for a picnic bottle
provisioning:Krater.story: Krater is the old guide's address for a bottle to take away: a short list of small Portuguese growers on Rua Conselheiro Bívar, a pedestrian street of the Baixa between the marina and Rua de Santo António, with a knowledgeable owner behind the counter. Ask for the Algarve's own grapes, a pale Negra Mole red or a Crato Branco, and carry it to the boat or across to Praia de Faro. Since October 2013 the street has also given its name to Bívar, an annual festival of design, shops and culture. We could not confirm in October 2026 that the shop still trades: check before you walk over.
provisioning:Krater.why: Come for a local Negra Mole or Crato Branco you will not find on the marina-front lists.

provisioning:Morgado do Quintão.name: Morgado do Quintão
provisioning:Morgado do Quintão.teaser: Organic vines between Silves and Lagoa, and lunch under an olive tree said to be 2,000 years old
provisioning:Morgado do Quintão.story: The olive tree is what people remember: about seven metres tall and as wide round, reckoned to be some 2,000 years old, with the tasting table set in its shade when the weather holds. Around it, Filipe Caldas de Vasconcellos farms the family's old estate with the winemaker Joana Maçanita, who works with local grapes and a light hand in the cellar. The modern wines only began with the 2016 vintage. Taste the dry-farmed Crato Branco, the white the Algarve now pins its name on, and the pale Palhete rosé. It is about an hour west of Faro, so make the day of it.
provisioning:Morgado do Quintão.why: Book the lunch under the olive tree, and taste the Crato Branco at the table.
facts: Estrada das Relíquias, between Silves and Lagoa; about 45 min to 1 h by car west of Faro

provisioning:Cabrita Wines.name: Cabrita Wines
provisioning:Cabrita Wines.teaser: The Silves family winery that bottles the Algarve's own red grape, Negra Mole, in every colour
provisioning:Cabrita Wines.story: José André Cabrita planted Crato Branco, Negra Mole and Castelão at Quinta da Vinha outside Silves in 1977, on a family farm that grew fruit before it grew wine; the first bottle under the Cabrita name came in 2007. The family now works about 16 hectares across three plots, and no one in the region has backed Negra Mole harder: as rosé, as a light red, as a sparkling wine, and in 2016 as a red that took a gold medal in Brussels. The visit walks the vines, the winery and the barrel room, then sits you down with four wines, local cheeses and charcuterie.
provisioning:Cabrita Wines.why: Taste the Negra Mole as red and as sparkling side by side: the same grape, two different wines.
facts: Quinta da Vinha, Silves; about 45 min by car west of Faro

provisioning:Casa do Medronho.name: Casa do Medronho, Marmelete
provisioning:Casa do Medronho.teaser: A village house in the Serra de Monchique where a copper still turns strawberry-tree fruit into spirit
provisioning:Casa do Medronho.story: Medronho is distilled from the red, rough-skinned berries of the strawberry tree that grows wild on the Serra de Monchique, picked in autumn and fermented for weeks before the copper still. Marmelete, a village on the western side of the hills, opened its Casa do Medronho in 2015: a traditional distillery rebuilt so visitors can watch the still run in season, with panels following the fruit from picking to bottle, tastings, and a counter selling local spirit, sausages and honey. From the house a route leads out to licensed farm distilleries; the municipality counts about 80 of them. The Festa do Medronho in Monchique belongs to the calendar.
provisioning:Casa do Medronho.why: Come in late autumn, when the stills are lit, and taste it at room temperature.
facts: Marmelete, Serra de Monchique; about 1 h 30 by car north-west of Faro

walks:Round the walls, gate to gate.name: Round the walls, gate to gate
walks:Round the walls, gate to gate.teaser: In by the Arco da Vila at first light, out by the Arco do Repouso, then along the ramparts to the marina
walks:Round the walls, gate to gate.story: Go in through the Arco da Vila early, while the town is empty. Cross the Largo da Sé, past the Bishop's Palace, and down to the Convento da Assunção. Leave by the Arco do Repouso, the eastern gate, flanked by two projecting Moorish towers; tradition says Afonso III rested here after taking Faro in 1249. Outside, follow the ramparts above the lagoon, where the salt pans and the islands lie flat on the water, then turn along the marina to the Jardim Manuel Bívar. On the way, the smells: salt, boat tar, the first sardine grill, coffee from Café Aliança, open since 1908.
walks:Round the walls, gate to gate.why: The rampart stretch outside the Arco do Repouso, with the whole lagoon below you.
facts: The Arco da Vila, on the Jardim Manuel Bívar side of the old town

walks:The Ludo trail and the salt pans.name: The Ludo trail and the salt pans
walks:The Ludo trail and the salt pans.teaser: A flat lagoon loop past salt pans where the flamingo flocks grow from October to March
walks:The Ludo trail and the salt pans.story: The Caminho do Ludo runs flat through the western end of the Ria Formosa natural park, created in 1987: brackish lagoons, pine and eucalyptus, the São Lourenço wetland, then the square mirrors of the salt pans. A few greater flamingos stay all year, but the big flocks are here from October to March, so late autumn is the right moment. Look for spoonbills, avocets and godwits working the mud. At dawn the birds feed before walkers and joggers arrive, and the pans turn pink and grey in the low light. There is a bird hide on the São Lourenço side.
walks:The Ludo trail and the salt pans.why: Dawn at the salt pans, with binoculars, for the flamingos feeding in the half-light.
facts: The Ludo side, west of Faro airport; the long version runs on to São Lourenço and Quinta do Lago
About 3 to 4 hours for the whole loop; the salt pans are near the start

calas:Ilha Deserta.name: Ilha Deserta
calas:Ilha Deserta.teaser: A sand island with no roads and no houses, and a boardwalk to the southern tip of mainland Portugal
calas:Ilha Deserta.story: Its real name is Ilha da Barreta, but everyone calls it Deserta, and the name holds: no roads, no residents, one restaurant. The boat leaves from the old town's edge and threads the channels of the Ria Formosa between mudflats and salt marsh. On the island a wooden boardwalk crosses the dunes to Cabo de Santa Maria, counted as the southernmost point of continental Portugal; the lighthouse you see across the channel stands on Culatra. Then walk the ocean beach, kilometres of it, with herons and spoonbills on the lagoon side. In late October the Atlantic is cooling from about 20°C. Estaminé, the island's restaurant, has its own card; check that it is open before you go out of season.
calas:Ilha Deserta.why: Walk the boardwalk to Cabo de Santa Maria, then have the ocean beach to yourself.
facts: Animaris boat from the Porta Nova pier at the edge of the old town, about 45 minutes; winter sailings are reduced: check the times (Oct 2026)

calas:Culatra and the Farol.name: Culatra and the Farol
calas:Culatra and the Farol.teaser: A lagoon island of fishermen's houses and sand lanes, with a lighthouse and an ocean beach at its tip
calas:Culatra and the Farol.story: Culatra is a barrier island with no cars and two settlements. Culatra village is where the fishing families live: low houses and sand lanes instead of tarmac. Farol, at the western end, grew up around the lighthouse of Cabo de Santa Maria and looks over the channel to Ilha Deserta. From either landing a short walk across the island brings you to the ocean beach, long, open and swept by the Atlantic swell. In late October the sea is around 18-20°C and falling: a short, bracing swim. Boats run all year from Olhão, but much less often in winter, and many island cafés shut for the season.
calas:Culatra and the Farol.why: Walk from the Farol landing to the lighthouse, then cross to the ocean side for the swim.

calas:Ilha de Tavira.name: Ilha de Tavira
calas:Ilha de Tavira.teaser: A few minutes by boat from the Quatro Águas jetty to kilometres of sand, and the anchors of Barril
calas:Ilha de Tavira.story: The boat from Quatro Águas leaves from where the Gilão river opens into the lagoon, past the salt pans and the moored fishing boats, and the crossing is over almost before you sit down. On the other side a short path leads to the ocean beach, which runs west for kilometres; walk it far enough, about 5 km, and you reach Praia do Barril and its rows of rusted anchors, whose story is told in the guide's food-history pages. Come back at the end of the day and stay on the jetty: the island goes dark against the sky and the boats come in to moor.
calas:Ilha de Tavira.why: The last hour on the Quatro Águas jetty, with the island in silhouette and the boats coming in.
facts: Boat from the Cais das Quatro Águas, about 2 km from Tavira centre; the only route running in winter, about 3-4 sailings a day, about EUR 2 return (Oct 2026 listings; check the operator's timetable). Barril also by footbridge from Pedras d'El Rei

around:Olhão.name: Olhão
around:Olhão.teaser: The Algarve's biggest fishing port, its flat-roofed white houses, and the boats out to the islands
around:Olhão.story: Olhão works for a living: it is the largest fishing port in the Algarve. The two red-brick market halls of 1916 stand on the front. Behind them is the Bairro dos Pescadores, a tangle of narrow lanes and cube-shaped white houses with flat roof terraces, built in a style people link to North Africa, with washing and sometimes fish drying on the balconies. From the piers beside the market, boats cross to Armona and to Culatra. Come on a Saturday morning, early.
around:Olhão.why: Get lost in the Bairro dos Pescadores lanes after the market, before the town has its lunch.
facts: About 10 km east of Faro: a short train ride on the Algarve line (about 10-15 minutes; check the timetable), or about 15 minutes by car
A morning; a full day with a boat to the islands

around:Tavira.name: Tavira
around:Tavira.teaser: A river town of churches and tiled houses, crossed by a seven-arched bridge everyone calls Roman
around:Tavira.story: The Gilão runs through Tavira, and everyone crosses it on the Ponte Romana: seven low arches, closed to cars since 1989. Climb from the river to the castle walls and the Igreja de Santa Maria do Castelo, rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake, with the roofs of the town below. Tavira has more churches than any other Algarve town, so you will pass a bell tower at almost every turn. Look for the old nora, a Moorish water-wheel, near Rua de Santo Estêvão. In the evening walk down to the Quatro Águas jetty, where the river meets the lagoon and the salt pans.
around:Tavira.why: Stand on the bridge at dusk, then climb to the castle for the roofs.
facts: About 35 km east of Faro: about 35 minutes by train (old guide; check the timetable) or by car
A day, with the boat to Ilha de Tavira
The castle and Santa Maria do Castelo; the bridge over the Gilão
The 'Roman' bridge: some say it stands on Roman road foundations, others that it is medieval; the present span is usually dated to a rebuilding in 1667

around:Loulé.name: Loulé
around:Loulé.teaser: A 1908 market hall in neo-Moorish dress, and a Saturday when the growers fill the streets around it
around:Loulé.story: Loulé's market opened in June 1908, designed by Alfredo Costa Campos to show off a prosperous town: four pavilions, a cupola at each corner, Moorish arches picked out in raspberry red against cream walls. A 2007 restoration finally built two towers that had been drawn in the original plans. On Saturday mornings the growers spill out into the surrounding streets with oranges, pomegranates, almonds, dried figs, carob and honey, and on the edge of town a larger market sets up that locals call the Mercado dos Ciganos. Walk up to the castle walls afterwards and on to the coppersmiths' street. Festival MED belongs to the calendar.
around:Loulé.why: Saturday morning, for the market hall and the growers' stalls outside it at the same time.
facts: About 20-30 minutes by car north-west of Faro

around:Sagres and Cabo de São Vicente.name: Sagres and Cabo de São Vicente
around:Sagres and Cabo de São Vicente.teaser: Cliffs dropping into the Atlantic at Europe's south-western corner, and Henry the Navigator's fortress
around:Sagres and Cabo de São Vicente.story: At the end of the Algarve the land stops in sheer cliffs, the wind rarely drops, and the lighthouse of Cabo de São Vicente marks the south-western corner of mainland Europe. A few kilometres east, the Fortaleza de Sagres fills a flat headland: walls on the landward side, the open sea on the other three. It is tied to Henry the Navigator, was battered by the 1755 tsunami, and drew 427,817 visitors in 2023, making it Portugal's second most visited monument. At the cape, Wolfgang and Petra Bald, emigrants from Nuremberg, have sold 'the last bratwurst before America' from a grill wagon since 1996, certificate included; 2026 trading not confirmed.
around:Sagres and Cabo de São Vicente.why: The cliff edge at Cabo de São Vicente in the late light, with nothing between you and America.
